question: What is the primary purpose of standardized anatomical terminology in nursing?

options.A: Speeding up the discharge process for stable patients
options.B: Simplifying complex surgical instruments for daily use
options.C: Ensuring clear communication among healthcare providers
options.D: Reducing the cost of patient hospital admissions

explanation: Standardized terms create a universal language that prevents confusion during patient handovers and documentation. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h1)

question: In medical terms, what does the prefix 'inter-' mean?
explanation: You've got this! The prefix inter- simply means 'between'—like the intercostal spaces found right between your ribs. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h1)

question: How should the palms face when a person is in the standard anatomical position?
explanation: Think of standing straight with your arms at your sides and turning your palms out so they face forward. That's the universal anatomical stance! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h2)

question: Why do nurses always assess patients using a universal anatomical position as a reference?

options.A: To maintain consistent and accurate clinical documentation
options.B: To prevent the spread of hospital-acquired infections
options.C: To reduce the time required to complete a bed bath
options.D: To make physical examinations more comfortable for patients

explanation: Using one standard body position ensures that when you write notes, every other nurse or doctor reading them pictures the exact same thing. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h2)

question: Which anatomical plane cuts the body into front and back parts?
explanation: The frontal plane (also called the coronal plane) acts like a vertical slice separating the front of the body from the back. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h3)

question: A CT scan image that slices horizontally across the abdomen uses which anatomical plane?
explanation: Great job! Transverse planes run horizontally across the body, giving us those neat cross-sectional views like rings on a tree trunk. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which directional term describes a body part that is located higher up, closer to the head?
explanation: Think 'superior' like being at the top. It means a structure is higher up or closer to the head than another part. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h4)

question: How is the knee positioned relative to the ankle?
explanation: Because the knee is closer to the center of the body (the trunk) than the ankle, we call it proximal. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h4)

question: Which muscle acts as a divider between the chest cavity and the tummy area (abdominopelvic cavity)?
explanation: The diaphragm is that dome-shaped breathing muscle that neatly separates your chest (thoracic) cavity from your belly area. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h5)

question: Which organs are safely housed entirely inside the dorsal body cavity?
explanation: The dorsal cavity protects our central nervous system, meaning it contains our brain up top and the spinal cord running down the back. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h5)

question: When a patient has appendicitis, where do we usually check for sharp pain?
explanation: Your appendix hangs out in the right lower corner of your belly, so tenderness right there is a classic sign of appendicitis! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h6)

question: When mapping out the abdomen using the grid system, how many distinct regions do we get?
explanation: You get a nice tic-tac-toe board of nine distinct anatomical areas, making it much easier to pinpoint tummy pain! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h6)
